title: A class is a blueprint, and an object is the actual instance created from it.
when_to_show: When distinguishing between class definitions and object creation
body: A class can be thought of as a blueprint for creating values of the same type. Just because you define `class Dog:` doesn’t mean a dog is created right away.
detail: An actual object is created when you call the class name, such as `dog = Dog()`. When reading code, look at the class block to see what attributes and methods it defines, and then follow along to the line where the object is created to see where the actual value is generated. This card is not intended to help you memorize object-oriented concepts by rote, but rather to serve as a supplementary explanation for understanding how `class`, `object`, `self`, `__init__`, `attribute`, and `method` are interconnected in actual Python code.

title: `self` refers to the current object itself
when_to_show: When you see code like `self.name` inside a method
body: `self` refers to the current object on which the method is being executed. When you read `dog.name` or call `dog.speak()`, you can think of `self` inside the `speak` method as referring to the `dog` object.
detail: Therefore, `self.name` is an expression that reads the `name` attribute of the current object. Rather than memorizing `self` as if it were a separate piece of information, it’s important to understand it in the context of which object’s method is being called. This card is not intended to make object-oriented programming difficult to memorize, but rather to serve as a supplementary explanation for understanding how `class`, `object`, `self`, `__init__`, `attribute`, and `method` are connected in actual Python code.

title: __init__ is executed the first time an object is created.
when_to_show: When looking at the __init__ method inside a class
body: Calling Dog('Momo') normally lets __new__ create an instance and then __init__ initialize its state. __init__ is commonly called a constructor, but it does not itself create and return the instance.
detail: Follow arguments into parameters and then into self attributes.

title: An attribute is a label associated with an object.
when_to_show: When you see dot notation like `obj.name` or `obj.score`,
body: An attribute can be thought of as a label for a value held by an object.
detail: `student.name` is an expression that reads the `name` value held by the `student` object, and `student.score = 90` is an expression that creates or changes the `score` attribute. Unlike local variables inside a function, attributes remain attached to the object. When using dot notation, you must verify which attribute of which object you are reading or modifying.

title: A method is treated like a function attached to an object.
when_to_show: When you see code in the form of `obj.method()`
body: A method is a function defined within a class that operates on an object. Functions where the first parameter is `self`—such as `def speak(self):`—can be called by the object.
detail: When `dog.speak()` is executed, the `self` inside `speak` becomes `dog`. Methods can read or modify attributes and return calculation results. When reading code, first check which object `self` refers to within a method.

title: Objects created from the same class each have their own attributes.
when_to_show: When creating multiple objects of the same class
body: You can create multiple objects of the same class, but each object can have its own attributes. If you create `a = User('A')` and `b = User('B')`, `a.name` could be `A` and `b.name` could be `B`.
detail: Even though they are created from the same blueprint, their actual values are managed separately. When reading code, you must not get confused about which object’s attribute is being printed. This card is not intended to help you memorize object-oriented concepts by rote, but rather to serve as a supplementary explanation for understanding how `class`, `object`, `self`, `__init__`, `attribute`, and `method` are interconnected in actual Python code.

title: A class variable is a shared value associated with the class.
when_to_show: When looking at variables assigned directly within a class
body: A class variable is stored on the class and instances can share it through attribute lookup. An instance assignment can shadow it, and a mutable class variable such as a list can create unintended shared state.
detail: Distinguish common configuration from per-instance state.

title: Object code is read in the order of creation, storage, and invocation.
when_to_show: When you need to quickly grasp the overall flow of a class's code
body: Object-oriented code is easier to trace as class definition → object creation → attribute storage → method call. Read the blueprint first, then follow what values and behavior the actual object uses.
detail: Inside the class block, identify the attributes and methods it defines. At a line such as dog = Dog('Momo'), __init__ commonly sets the object's initial attributes. Later, dot expressions such as dog.name or dog.speak() show which object's data is read or which method is called.
